name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Saturday 28 October 1967

clue.text: Stars of the literary world

blocks.note: surface reading: famous writers, the celebrities of literature; setter's reading: clusters of stars in the sky
in print, the same word names a triangle of three little star marks set in a text

explanation.surface: The celebrated big names of the book world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stars' suggests famous authors, but the answer is literal: an asterism is a group of stars, and also the printer's sign of three asterisks.
explanation.definitionFit: An asterism is a small pattern of stars in the sky, and also a typographic mark of three star symbols.

clue.text: He does a dance in sand

definitions.text: He does a dance in sand

blocks.note: surface reading: a music-hall sand dance, the comic shuffle performed on a sprinkled stage
setter's reading: a desert dweller, whose whole life is spent among the dunes

explanation.surface: A performer doing a soft-shoe shuffle across a sanded stage.
explanation.walkthrough: The music-hall 'sand dance' was a comic routine in mock-Egyptian costume, so the setter points from the stage act to a real desert people.
explanation.definitionFit: An Arab is a person from the Arabic-speaking peoples, traditionally pictured living in the desert lands of the Middle East.

clue.text: Heard at the furniture makers' conference?

definitions.text: Heard at the furniture makers' conference?

blocks.clueFragment: Heard at the furniture makers' conference?
blocks.note: surface reading: the shop talk exchanged by cabinet makers at a trade meeting
setter's reading: carpenters naturally discuss what they build, chiefly dining furniture

explanation.surface: Chatter overheard at a gathering of furniture manufacturers.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase normally means informal chat over a meal; the question mark flags a literal reading as conversation about tables.
explanation.definitionFit: Table talk is the relaxed conversation people have while sitting at a meal together.

clue.text: It is scarcely in evidence

blocks.note: surface reading: something barely visible, hardly present at all
setter's reading: an adverb meaning seldom, the thing said of anything hardly ever seen

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like a description of an object; it is really a hint at an adverb close to 'scarcely'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that happens rarely happens seldom or infrequently, so it is hardly ever seen.

clue.text: He is absorbed in parsimony

definitions.note: a man, standing for a man's name

indicators.note: something absorbed sits wholly inside another thing, so the name lies within the longer word

blocks.note: the five letters after the opening PAR of this word

explanation.surface: A man wholly given over to stinginess.
explanation.definitionFit: Simon is a common masculine first name, so it can stand for a man referred to only as 'he'.

clue.text: The defence has it in the bag

definitions.text: The defence has it in the bag

blocks.clueFragment: The defence has it in the bag
blocks.note: surface reading: a lawyer or team whose case is already won, as good as certain
setter's reading: a military barricade of filled bags, plus the loose material packed inside them

explanation.surface: The defending side is sure to win.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the bag' means certain, but here it is literal: sandbags piled up as a defensive wall hold the answer inside them.
explanation.definitionFit: Sand is the loose granular material packed into sacks to make sandbags for fortifications and flood walls.

clue.text: A return service in India

definitions.note: a phrase describing a place, standing for a region of India

indicators.note: to return is to go back the way you came, so the word is read from its end

blocks.note: taken as written
a Mass is a church service

explanation.surface: A tennis return of serve during a match played in India.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return service' reads as a tennis shot, but 'return' acts on the church service that follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: Assam is a state in north-eastern India, famous for growing tea.

clue.text: A weakness in that case in Asia

indicators.note: the second 'in' places one word inside the continent named after it

blocks.note: taken as written
'in that case' means then, as in 'then we'll go'

explanation.surface: A frailty observed in a particular Asian case.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'in' belongs to the phrase 'in that case'; only the second 'in' does the inserting.
explanation.definitionFit: Asthenia is the medical term for bodily weakness or loss of strength.

clue.text: Flora's reserve

definitions.note: plant life in general, standing for one garden flower

blocks.note: first meaning: a scented garden flower, the gillyflower
second meaning: a supply kept in store for future use

explanation.surface: A woman called Flora keeps something set aside.
explanation.walkthrough: Flora looks like a woman's name; read as plant life, it points to a garden flower.
explanation.definitionFit: Stock is both a fragrant cottage-garden plant and a store of goods held ready for use.

clue.text: Bad men, made to smart, since reformed

indicators.note: something reformed is formed again in a new shape, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Wrongdoers who were punished and have since mended their ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reformed' suggests villains turned good, but it is the signal to rearrange the ten letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Miscreants are wrongdoers or villains, people who behave badly or break the law.

clue.text: Colour of novel perpetuity

definitions.note: a description of a book title, standing for the name in it

blocks.note: first meaning: a warm yellowish-orange shade
second meaning: the heroine of Kathleen Winsor's 1944 bestseller Forever ..., 'forever' being perpetuity

explanation.surface: A colour belonging to some new idea of eternity.
explanation.walkthrough: Forever Amber was a racy 1940s historical novel; 'perpetuity' stands for its first word, leaving the second as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Amber is a golden yellow-brown shade, named after the fossil resin, and the heroine's name in a famous novel.

clue.text: "I'll speak in a little voice" (M.N. Dream)

definitions.text: "I'll speak in a little voice" (M.N. Dream)

blocks.note: a line of Bottom's from Shakespeare's comedy with one word missing
A Midsummer Night's Dream; the missing word is an adjective meaning huge or outrageous

explanation.walkthrough: Bottom, wanting to play Thisbe too, promises: 'I'll speak in a monstrous little voice', a comic contradiction.
explanation.definitionFit: Monstrous means enormous or outrageous; Bottom uses it loosely as an intensifier, meaning 'very'.

clue.text: Winner takes all but this

blocks.note: surface reading: the familiar rule that the victor collects every prize
setter's reading: a kind of horse race in which the winning horse must afterwards be offered at auction, so its owner may not keep it

explanation.surface: The winner collects everything except one thing.
explanation.walkthrough: In a selling race, or selling plate, the winner is put up for sale after the race, so the winner takes everything except a guarantee of keeping the horse.
explanation.definitionFit: A selling race is a low-grade horse race whose winning horse must be put up for sale by auction afterwards.

clue.text: Faint heart fails in the upkeep of this bird

definitions.text: Faint heart fails in the upkeep of this bird

blocks.note: surface reading: the proverb 'faint heart never won fair lady', a timid person losing out
setter's reading: a British idiom about keeping something up to stay cheerful, where that something is also a short name for a tree-drilling bird

explanation.surface: A timid owner fails to look after a pet bird properly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep your pecker up' is British slang for keep your spirits up; a faint-hearted person fails to do so. 'Upkeep' splits into keeping it up.
explanation.definitionFit: Pecker is old British slang for courage or spirits, and also a short name for a woodpecker.

clue.text: They should have a quick send-off

definitions.text: They should have a quick send-off

blocks.clueFragment: They should have a quick send-off
blocks.note: surface reading: people who deserve a brisk farewell or a speedy funeral
setter's reading: official messages, which by their nature are sent off with all speed

explanation.walkthrough: 'Send-off' suggests a farewell party, but the things meant are messages whose name itself implies haste.
explanation.definitionFit: Despatches are official reports or messages sent swiftly, such as military reports from the front.

clue.text: Passed unanimously at early peace conferences

definitions.text: Passed unanimously at early peace conferences

blocks.note: surface reading: a motion approved by every delegate's vote
setter's reading: North American treaty councils, where a ceremonial tobacco bowl was handed round to everyone

explanation.walkthrough: 'Passed' suggests a vote, but the thing was physically passed hand to hand: the peace pipe smoked at Native American councils.
explanation.definitionFit: A pipe is a tube with a bowl for smoking tobacco, as in the calumet or peace pipe shared to seal agreements.

clue.text: He is back in church

definitions.note: a man, standing for a man's name

indicators.note: going back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the word is read from its end

blocks.note: the nave is the main body of a church, where the congregation sits

explanation.surface: A man has returned to attending church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back in church' sounds like a lapsed churchgoer returning; it is the part of a church read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Evan is a masculine first name, the Welsh form of John, so it can stand for 'he'.

clue.text: A sad spirit growing in suburbia

definitions.note: a describing phrase, standing for a plant that grows there

indicators.note: something growing is changing its form as it develops, so these letters take a new shape

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A gloomy ghost is thriving among the suburban houses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Growing' does double duty, signalling the rearrangement and describing the plant. The aspidistra was the classic, slightly dreary parlour plant of the suburban home.
explanation.definitionFit: The aspidistra is a tough leafy houseplant, famously kept in front rooms of suburban British homes.

clue.text: They go to sea four times a year

definitions.text: They go to sea four times a year

blocks.note: surface reading: sailors who set out on voyages
setter's reading: put the boys after the word sea and you get the four divisions of the year

explanation.surface: Sailors who put to sea once every quarter.
explanation.walkthrough: The male children 'go to' the word sea, joining it to make spring, summer, autumn and winter's collective name.
explanation.definitionFit: Sons are male children; joined after sea they form the name for the year's four quarters.

clue.text: "Before the starry of Jove's Court My mansion is" (Milton)

definitions.text: "Before the starry of Jove's Court My mansion is" (Milton)

blocks.clueFragment: "Before the starry of Jove's Court My mansion is"
blocks.note: the opening lines of Milton's masque Comus with a word missing
the Attendant Spirit says this; the missing word is the doorstep or entrance of a building

explanation.walkthrough: Comus opens: 'Before the starry threshold of Jove's Court / My mansion is, where those immortal shapes...'.
explanation.definitionFit: A threshold is the sill or doorway at the entrance of a building, here the gateway of heaven.

clue.text: What's unusual about an ordinary seaman?

definitions.note: a phrase meaning 'something unusual'; the answer is an adjective

blocks.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, is the usual crossword sailor
ordinary means usual or standard

explanation.surface: Asking what is odd about a lowly ordinary seaman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ordinary seaman' is a real naval rank, but the two words split apart. The pieces come in the opposite order to the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Abnormal means departing from what is usual or typical, which is what unusual describes.

clue.text: Not for the pig-buyer's wife

blocks.note: surface reading: the proverb warning against buying a pig in a poke, a sack you cannot see into
setter's reading: a woman's hat with a projecting brim, named with the same sack-word

explanation.walkthrough: A poke is an old word for a bag; never buy a pig in a poke. The hat shares the word but is worn by women, not bought by pig dealers.
explanation.definitionFit: A poke bonnet is a woman's bonnet with a projecting front brim, fashionable in the nineteenth century.

clue.text: Sandy's pluck?

blocks.note: surface reading: the courage of a man called Sandy, the stock Scottish name
setter's reading: courage that also suggests sand, since the word means both fine particles of stone and bravery

explanation.walkthrough: Sandy is a typical Scottish nickname for Alexander; the courage word also means coarse sand.
explanation.definitionFit: Grit means determined courage and also small particles of stone or sand.

clue.text: Not the happy hunting ground of the sniper

definitions.text: Not the happy hunting ground of the sniper

blocks.note: surface reading: a favourite place to hunt, or the Native American heaven
setter's reading: a hunter of snipe would not seek the bird in a roadside drain, though a ragged street child is named after both

explanation.walkthrough: A guttersnipe is a ragged street child; despite the name, no one hunting snipe would look for it in the drain at the roadside.
explanation.definitionFit: A gutter is the channel along the edge of a road that carries away rainwater.

clue.text: Where to get the best gratuity?

definitions.text: Where to get the best gratuity?

blocks.note: surface reading: asking which place pays the most generous tips
setter's reading: the very top tip, which reversed into a phrase means first-rate

explanation.walkthrough: The best tip is the 'top tip'; flip the words and you have the adjective for excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiptop means excellent or of the very highest quality, just as the best of anything is.

clue.text: Venetian artist makes capital in an island

blocks.note: first meaning: ... Vecchio or his grand-nephew ... Giovane, painters of the Venetian school
second meaning: the capital city of Majorca, in the Balearic Islands

explanation.surface: A painter from Venice earns a fortune on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Makes capital' looks like making money; split off, 'capital in an island' is a city.
explanation.definitionFit: Palma is the surname of two Venetian Renaissance painters and the chief city of the Spanish island of Majorca.

clue.text: Old bean explains himself with some force

blocks.note: introducing himself he says 'I'm', the contraction of I am
a pulse is an edible seed such as a bean or lentil; 'old bean' is a dated British form of address

explanation.surface: An old chap justifies himself quite forcefully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old bean' is old-fashioned British slang for 'old chap'; here the bean literally says who he is.
explanation.definitionFit: An impulse is a sudden driving force or push, and in physics a force acting for a short time.

clue.text: He is able to be dispirited

definitions.text: He is able to be dispirited

blocks.note: surface reading: a man who is capable of feeling low
setter's reading: this hoarder followed by the word able makes an adjective for wretched or unhappy

explanation.walkthrough: Add ABLE to the hoarder and you get MISERABLE, which is what dispirited means.
explanation.definitionFit: A miser is someone who hoards money and spends as little as possible.

clue.text: None of it is good, we are told

definitions.text: None of it is good, we are told

blocks.note: surface reading: a complaint that all of something is bad
setter's reading: the proverb 'no tidings is good tidings', that hearing nothing is a good sign

explanation.walkthrough: The saying is 'no news is good news': having none of it is the good thing.
explanation.definitionFit: News is fresh information about recent events, reported or passed on to others.

clue.text: She's obliging, but looks fishy (4). (Answer Monday)

blocks.note: first meaning: a charwoman, a cleaning lady who obliges by doing housework
second meaning: a fish of the trout family found in cold lakes

explanation.surface: A helpful woman who nevertheless seems suspicious.
explanation.walkthrough: A char is British for a cleaning woman, often called an obliger; 'fishy' usually means suspicious, but here she literally looks like a fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Char is short for charwoman, a hired house cleaner, and also the name of a trout-like freshwater fish.

clue.text: Useful people in Hunts?

blocks.note: surface reading: helpful folk, of the sort a wife or partner is called in the Bible
setter's reading: a hunt gathering is a meet; Hunts is also short for the English county of Huntingdonshire

explanation.walkthrough: A helpmeet is a helpful partner, from Genesis; split it and a hunt's assembly, a meet, appears.
explanation.definitionFit: Helpmeets are helpful companions or partners, especially spouses, from the 'help meet' of Genesis.

clue.text: Part of what we should do unto others

indicators.note: the answer is made of part of the words that come after, sitting across two of them

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A fragment of the Golden Rule about treating others as yourself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part' is both the definition and the start of the signal. There is a sly nod to 'a tooth for a tooth', a harsher rule of conduct.
explanation.definitionFit: A tooth is a part of the mouth, or one of the projecting parts of a cog or comb.

clue.text: He is slow to move house

definitions.text: He is slow to move house

blocks.note: surface reading: a sluggish person who keeps putting off a move
setter's reading: a creature that literally carries its home on its back as it creeps along

explanation.surface: Someone who takes his time about relocating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Move house' means relocate, but this creature moves its house every time it moves at all, slowly.
explanation.definitionFit: A snail is a slow-moving mollusc carrying a coiled shell that serves as its home.

clue.text: One likely to be thrilled at getting on the Board!

definitions.text: One likely to be thrilled at getting on the Board!

blocks.clueFragment: One likely to be thrilled at getting on the Board!
blocks.note: surface reading: an ambitious person delighted to be appointed a company director
setter's reading: a plank ridden on breaking waves, which gives its rider a thrill

explanation.surface: An executive overjoyed at being made a company director.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Board' suggests a boardroom; the exclamation mark flags the wave-riding plank instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A surf-rider is someone who rides breaking waves standing on a surfboard.
